title: Tourists in Our Own Backyard
summary: A writer, a professor, and an overdue mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge in Concord. Our photographs and watercolors, local history, a map, and practical access notes.
search: The journal / New England Concord, Massachusetts · Time for two Tourists in Our Own Backyard A mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge. A writer, a professor, three years living nearby—and a little literary pilgrimage we somehow hadn’t made. Our photographs, watercolors, local history, and the practical details for a visit of your own. October 21, 2026 · An AUsome Life Our date ↓The history ↓The watercolors ↓Map & directions ↓Access & visiting ↓Writer & book cards ↓ Louisa May Alcott’s resting place, from our own visit to Authors’ Ridge. I’m a writer. Dad is a professor. We’d lived here for three years.And somehow, we had never made the trek to Authors’ Ridge. On paper, we were very well qualified to have done this already. But a funny thing happens when you live near somewhere people travel to see: it becomes the place you can visit any time. And “any time” has a way of slipping behind everything that actually has a date on the calendar. So, for a little while this fall, we became tourists in our own backyard. Our date took us to Authors’ Ridge in Concord’s Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Louisa May Alcott, Henry David Thoreau, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ralph Waldo Emerson are buried. Familiar names, suddenly attached to very small, very human places. About the writers and the cemetery. The things people leave behind Look closely at the photographs. Around Louisa May Alcott’s marker are pencils, pinecones, stones and a pink rose. At Thoreau’s, more pencils lie among the roots and needles, beneath a little stone that simply says Henry. I find the pencils especially moving. Such ordinary things, brought to the graves of people whose words have lasted so long. To me, they look like small thank-yous: your work reached someone. Someone is still reading. Hawthorne’s marker has its own quiet simplicity. A rounded stone, a surname, sunlight and shadow. You can know a name for years and still feel differently about it when you stand in front of it, outdoors, at the scale of a person. Henry: a small marker, tree roots, and the things visitors have left. Hawthorne, in patches of sun and shade. In our photographs, the trees still hold plenty of green. A little gold is beginning to show. The ground has its own autumn palette: brown needles, gray stone, moss, a bright flower. There is enough to look at before you read a single name. Before the graves, there were evening walks One of my favorite pieces of this place’s history is that the writers knew it as a place to walk. The National Park Service records that Emerson, Thoreau, and Nathaniel and Sophia Hawthorne enjoyed evening walks in Sleepy Hollow before it became a cemetery. Before these woods held their graves, they held their evening walks. That makes a date here feel part of a much older habit: going outside together, looking around, letting a familiar landscape give you something to think about. Sleepy Hollow was dedicated on September 29, 1855, with an address by Emerson. Landscape architects Horace William Shaler Cleveland and Robert Morris Copeland planned paths and drives around the natural shape of the land, respecting its trees and plants. The Concord Free Public Library’s dedication exhibit describes that approach—and notes that the place already carried the name Sleepy Hollow before it was a burial ground. It belongs to the nineteenth-century tradition of rural or garden cemeteries, where landscape and remembrance meet. The winding roads and wooded setting are part of the history you have come to see. Read about the landscape. A little more of the neighborhood Concord’s history reaches much further back than the writers. The Concord Museum identifies the area as the original homelands of the Nipmuc, Massachusett and Pawtucket tribal nations, and recognizes Indigenous people’s continuing connection to this land. Nearby, the North Bridge holds another chapter: the battle of April 19, 1775. A visit to Concord can open onto many histories. Authors’ Ridge gave us plenty to notice on its own. Something lovely, close to home A date like this makes room for the people we are as well as the people we look after. I’m still a writer. Dad is still someone who loves ideas. And we are still two people who can go somewhere together and find things worth noticing. I like that the visit didn’t need to be elaborate to be worth remembering. A nearby place, a little curiosity, a few photographs. There is a particular pleasure in finally doing the thing that has been waiting so close to home. Three years was a long time to get around to it. I’m glad we finally went. From the photographsA little autumn sketchbook Three watercolor interpretations of our visit. The photographs above show the actual places; these companion illustrations hold their color and feeling. About our editorial artwork. In mid-fall, plan around the earlier dusk. Check current town rules and posted gate signs. Mobility, ground surfaces & the approach Authors’ Ridge is a hillside visit. The official tourism listing says the approach includes an incline. Our photographs show exposed roots, bare earth and pine needles around some markers. The town’s cemetery master plan acknowledges accessibility challenges from the hills and limited parking. Parking nearer the ridge may shorten the approach; it does not establish a level or step-free route to every grave. If you use a wheelchair, walker or stroller, or need to limit walking, ask the Cemetery Office about your specific route and parking needs before going: 978-318-3233. After rain, take extra care around wet leaves and roots. Restrooms & a place to regroup Plan a restroom stop in Concord Center. The Concord Visitor Center at 58 Main Street lists public bathrooms, and its access guide identifies accessible restrooms inside. Those two pages currently give different opening hours for the facilities. If access to a particular restroom matters to your visit, call 978-318-3061 to confirm availability. Sensory needs, pacing & family planning The photos here are from our date. They do not establish how this outing would work for another person or at another time. Outdoor space can still include other visitors, vehicles and maintenance sounds. If predictability helps, preview the photographs and town map, choose a short first stop, and keep an easy return to the car in your plan. If visiting with someone who uses AAC or other communication supports, keep their usual communication available and make room for “break,” “leave” and “all done.” For a date that depends on someone else covering care, our caregiver handover guide offers a place to put the essentials. Being a thoughtful visitor Sleepy Hollow is an active cemetery. Give funerals and people visiting loved ones plenty of space. Follow the roads and paths, respect the grave lots, and leave markers and existing objects undisturbed. The town prohibits gravestone rubbing. See the cemetery rules for the full visiting and photography guidance. Keep the rest of the date simple For readers who want a second stop, Concord Bookshop at 65 Main Street continues the literary theme. Main Streets Market & Cafe at 42 Main Street is another nearby option for coffee or a meal. Check each business’s current hours and any access arrangements you need. These are ideas for extending your own outing. Or let the cemetery visit be the whole date. One nearby place, finally seen together, can be plenty. title: A little Easter color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.
search: The journalBerlin, MassachusettsAn Easter field note The bunny had a few photo ideas of its own. A spring visit to Berlin FarmsA little Easter color.An egg hunt, a bunny with a few good poses, and a family photograph worth keeping.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier Easter visitPastel eggs across the lawn. White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. The family storyMap & visit detailsAccess & sensory notesMore photographs Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good part is right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door. title: A little Bristol blue.
summary: A family photograph from Bristol, Rhode Island, a short waterfront guide, and our experience practicing staying together safely.
search: The journalBristol, Rhode IslandFrom the family archives · October 19, 2026 An afternoon by the harborA little Bristol blue.Sailboats, stripes, and a much smaller James. A photograph from the family album, with a short guide for an afternoon on the waterfront.Looking through old photos and found this one. Apparently, we all got the memo about wearing blue.The three of us by the water. From an earlier family visit. From the albumThe waterfront guideStaying together safely Glad we took this one.Bristol, Rhode Island: sailboats, sparkling water, and a family afternoon by the harbor. There is James in front, with the boats behind us and the sun on the water.There is a practical detail in the photograph, too. James and I were each holding a voluntary walking handle as we practiced staying together safely. Nothing was attached to him; there was no tether or restraint, and he could let go at any time.For our family, it was one way to practice while getting out and enjoying the community. Every child and family has different needs, and what worked for us may not feel right or be appropriate for someone else. It was one small part of our experience, alongside close supervision.Mostly, I am glad we have this picture. An afternoon by the water with my two favorite people. Original editorial illustration, inspired by Bristol. An imagined harbor scene, separate from our family photograph. A small plan for a day outAlong the waterfront.These are researched ideas for a visit today, rather than a list of places we visited on the afternoon in our photograph.Start at Independence Park.At 419–459 Thames Street, this four-acre park overlooks Bristol Harbor and marks the southern end of the East Bay Bike Path. The state tourism listing includes walkways and public restrooms; check restroom availability for your visit. A good starting point for watching the boats without committing to a long walk.Independence Park visitor informationTake a waterfront wander.The town points visitors to the boardwalk behind Stone Harbour condominiums, leading toward Rockwell Park and the Maritime Center. Choose a short stretch, stop for the view, and turn back whenever you like.Bristol’s official places guideTry a little of the bike path.The East Bay Bike Path runs 13.8 miles between Providence and Bristol. You do not have to tackle the whole thing: a short out-and-back from Independence Park can be enough. Cyclists share the path, so plan the support and space your family needs.East Bay Bike Path detailsMake Audubon a separate stop.The Audubon Nature Center and Aquarium at 1401 Hope Street has exhibits, walking trails and a boardwalk toward Narragansett Bay. Audubon describes its facility and trails as accessible. Check opening hours, admission and closure announcements before heading over.Audubon visitor informationBefore you go: check parking signs, restroom access and waterfront conditions. Bristol announced funding for seawall work at Independence Park and the Maritime Center in October 2026; the notice does not establish a closure schedule, so check local updates before visiting. Waterfront routes can include open edges, docks and boat activity.Official visitor sources checked October 19, 2026. This is a family recollection with a researched guide, not a current accessibility audit. Town seawall project notice. About the walking handle & practicing staying together safelyWe each held part of the handle, with James choosing to hold his. It gave us a way to practice walking together. Unexpected separation can become dangerous quickly, even with attentive caregivers.A similar style is called Hold-On Handles. This link shows the type of product, not a confirmed match for ours; current stock and suitability need checking.In a 2012 parent survey involving 1,218 autistic children, 49% were reported to have attempted elopement at least once after age four. That describes the surveyed group, not any individual child’s future. Read the original study in Pediatrics.The practical, hopeful part is making room for learning and finding supports that fit. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teaching safety skills alongside consistent adult supervision and an individual safety plan. Read the AAP’s guidance for families.A voluntarily held handle can be released at any moment. It cannot prevent unexpected separation or replace close supervision, particularly near water or traffic. We are sharing our experience, not general advice or a recommendation for restraint. Neither source establishes that a walking handle reduces elopement.Different people need different supports. For us, the point was getting out together and having opportunities to practice. Send a little Bristol to someone.Know someone who would enjoy an afternoon by the harbor? title: Burlington, at our pace.
summary: Our Burlington, Vermont trip in family photographs: Oakledge’s accessible treehouse, pool time at The Essex, Al’s French Frys, and a little holiday sparkle.
search: The journal / Vermont Burlington & Essex, Vermont · From the family album Burlington, at our pace. A treehouse, a swim, a stop at Al’s, and a little holiday sparkle. The small pieces of a Vermont trip worth keeping. Published October 16, 2026 · Photographs from an earlier family trip Pool time at The Essex. One of the good parts of getting away. The little storyThe treehouseOur Al’s stopAccess & planningUseful links Looking back through our Burlington photographs, I keep coming back to the smaller scenes: James in his Vermont shirt, the red booths at Al’s, a tree growing straight through a treehouse, and the two of them together in the pool. There is a very good Vermont trip in those pictures. A little time outside. Something familiar to eat. Water to get into. A Christmas tree dressed in black-and-white checks, because apparently even the decorations had packed appropriately. For our family, those ordinary pieces deserve room in the story. James loves the water, and the swimming photographs belong right alongside the sightseeing ones. The pool is part of the trip. A swim at The Essex The indoor pool at The Essex Resort & Spa has a lovely setting: wood walls, white beams, large windows, and blue-green water. In our photographs, James is wearing his life jacket with his dad beside him. In another, the two of them are wrapped up in a poolside hug. The photograph I would keep even without a travel story attached.White robes, white columns, and a little Vermont sunshine. The covered walkway is another detail I like in the album: two white robes, a long row of columns, and stripes of sunlight across the path. It is a useful reminder to ask about the journey between a room and a pool. The Essex’s spa is in a separate building; the practical notes below include the resort’s current access information. A treehouse you can actually get into At Oakledge Park in Burlington, the treehouse is built around the tree itself. Thick branches frame the view; the floorboards and rustic railings make a little room in the woods. James’s orange jacket stands out against all that weathered wood. Inside Oakledge’s treehouse, with the tree very much part of the room.A place to stop and look out. The access is part of what makes this place worth knowing about. Its builders describe it as a universally accessible community treehouse, created with the City of Burlington. That matters: the experience of being up among the branches should have room for more people. Our photographs capture the inside, rather than the full approach. For a future visit, I would check the route and current conditions with the park, especially after wet or icy weather. A lovely wooden walkway still has to contend with Vermont. Red booths and a Vermont shirt Our stop at Al’s French Frys in South Burlington looks exactly like the sort of place you hope to find on a New England trip: red booths, little pendant lights, and a black-and-white tiled floor. James is standing by the table in his Vermont shirt, with his device close by. A Vermont shirt for a Vermont stop. Al’s French Frys, South Burlington. That is a useful little travel detail in its own right. A communication device belongs at the table, within reach. New surroundings need not mean leaving familiar supports behind. Al’s current menu lists its namesake fries alongside burgers, sandwiches, and ice cream. The photo is our souvenir of the stop; for a particular food preference or allergy, check the current menu and preparation details directly. A little holiday sparkle A grin, red ornaments, and rather good checked ribbon. And then there is this picture. James, smiling beside the Christmas tree, blue Crocs and all. The ribbon is coordinated. The family travel wardrobe is taking a more independent approach. Looking through this trip again, what stands out is the variety without the need for a grand production: the treehouse, the pool, the diner, the decorations. There is plenty here for a family album, and plenty to build a manageable Burlington visit around. Take the useful details with youPlanning your own version These are memories from an earlier trip. The venue details below were checked on October 16, 2026; they describe what the venues currently publish, rather than facilities we personally tested. The Essex Resort & Spa · 70 Essex Way, EssexThe resort lists a year-round indoor pool. Its accessibility page says the spa and fitness center are in a separate building with paved wheelchair access, and that the pools and whirlpool have lifts. Ask about the exact route from your room, lift availability, changing arrangements, and current family swimming hours. We did not test the lifts or accessible rooms. Oakledge Park · Flynn Avenue, BurlingtonThe treehouse is documented as a universally accessible community treehouse. Burlington’s parks guidance says it is first come, first served and must remain open to the public. Burlington Wildways lists parking and accessible spaces near the Greenway. Check current parking charges, restroom availability, and the condition of the treehouse approach before you go. Al’s French Frys · 1251 Williston Road, South BurlingtonOur photo shows indoor booth seating. It does not establish wheelchair clearance, restroom access, or typical sound levels. Call 802-862-9203 for the seating or access details your family needs, and check the current menu and hours. A simple plan Choose one main outing, leave room for swimming, and keep a food stop flexible. These places are in Burlington, South Burlington, and Essex, so allow for driving between them. The photographs are a collection of trip moments, not a timed itinerary. For us, a useful planning question is: what does everyone need in order to enjoy the part we came for? A place to change, a device within reach, time to linger, and permission to finish while the day is still going well. Our hotel and pool checklist can help with the calls before booking. For a shorter outing, start with the shorter-visit plan.
